title: A task PID budget is not a shared user's RLIMIT_NPROC
applies_when: A Linux native-test or agent subprocess must spawn child commands under a small task budget, especially when it shares a real user ID with other workers and fork or clone fails with EAGAIN before target assertions run.
lesson: Check the accounting domain before transferring a resource limit. RLIMIT_NPROC counts existing processes and threads for the real user ID, not just the current test tree; a newly imposed limit can already be below that shared user's usage. Limits are inherited across fork and preserved across exec. A per-task budget needs an actual task-specific mechanism, such as a cgroup pids.max limit, with its hierarchy and current usage checked. Preserve process-creation failures as environment evidence rather than a target-code failure or no-bug result. Do not silently remove the limit and call execution equally isolated; qualify a fresh bounded route and retain the failed attempt.
avoid_when: EAGAIN alone does not identify RLIMIT_NPROC; cgroup, system and other admission limits can also prevent task creation. RLIMIT_NPROC is not enforced for real UID 0 or the documented privileged capabilities. A PID cgroup counts kernel tasks/threads, includes descendants and obeys ancestor limits; it is not memory, CPU, filesystem, network, GPU or kernel-exploit isolation. A successful fixed shell primitive is not qualification for arbitrary generated commands or a repository's native test suite.

evidence.note: Linux manual documents RLIMIT_NPROC's real-UID/thread accounting, EAGAIN, privilege exceptions and inheritance. This supports the limit mechanism, not a measured discovery or performance result.

Kernel documentation specifies the PID controller, pids.max/current, descendant accounting and hierarchical fork/clone enforcement. A task-specific cgroup must actually be established and inspected; merely naming a budget provides no isolation.
